issues.legal_issue: Mineral extraction from surface deposits constitutes mining operations, and land containing those deposits may be comprised in or appertain to a mine.
material_facts: The land contained large deposits of sand, a minor mineral.
The operators were excavating and removing the sand from the land.
issues.conclusion: The extraction and removal of the sand constituted mining operations, and the land was comprised in or appertained to a mine.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 2(j) of the Mines Act, 1952, and Sections 3(d) and 3(e) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, mining operations include activity to win a mineral whether on or beneath the earth’s surface. The word “any” in the definition of mine gives excavation a broad meaning in this context. The Court reiterated B. Dass v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

predicates.estate_vesting_retention_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether land containing minerals may be retained following the vesting of an estate.
predicates.mineral_bearing_land: The land contains a naturally occurring mineral deposit.
predicates.mineral_extraction_activity: An operator extracts or removes the mineral from the land, whether at the surface or below it.

issues.definition: When a vesting-related retention dispute concerns mineral-bearing land from which an operator extracts or removes the mineral, the land is treated as comprised in or appertaining to a mine.

issues.legal_issue: An intermediary does not directly work a mine when another operator conducts the mining under rights granted by the intermediary, and the special rule for mines prevails over the general right to retain qualifying land.
material_facts: The intermediary granted the respondents the right to conduct mining operations and remove the mineral in return for a periodic payment.
The respondents, rather than the intermediary or its representative, were working the mine immediately before vesting.
The intermediary claimed that it could retain the land through a licensee for a religious purpose.
issues.conclusion: The intermediary was not directly working the mine and could not retain the land; the rule governing mines prevailed over the claimed general retention right, even assuming the land was held through a licensee.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28 of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, permits retention only where the mine was directly worked by the intermediary immediately before vesting, meaning under the intermediary’s immediate control, management and supervision. Working through a lessee, licensee or other agency granted mining rights for periodic consideration is not direct working. Under Section 27, Chapter IV overrides contrary provisions elsewhere in the Act, so Section 28 prevails over Section 6(1)(i).

rule.if: estate_vesting_retention_dispute and mineral_bearing_land and intermediary_granted_mining_rights and outside_operator_worked_mine_at_vesting

predicates.estate_vesting_retention_dispute: The proceeding concerns an intermediary’s claimed right to retain land after an estate vests.
predicates.mineral_bearing_land: The land contains a mineral deposit that is worked as a mine.
predicates.intermediary_granted_mining_rights: The intermediary granted another person or agency the right to conduct mining operations and remove the mineral in return for periodic consideration.
predicates.outside_operator_worked_mine_at_vesting: A person or agency other than the intermediary conducted the mining immediately before vesting.

issues.definition: When an intermediary’s retention claim concerns mineral-bearing land worked immediately before vesting by an outside operator acting under rights granted by the intermediary, the intermediary cannot retain the mine.

issues.legal_issue: A grant of mineral-extraction rights is a lease rather than a licence when its substance gives the grantee a time-limited right to enjoy the land through mining and exclusive possession in return for periodic consideration.
material_facts: The agreement granted the respondents the right to raise, take out, remove and appropriate sand from the land.
The grant ran for a specified term and required a fixed annual payment irrespective of the quantity of sand extracted.
The agreement contemplated the respondents remaining in exclusive possession for the term and the grantor retaking possession at its end.
The agreement was labelled a licence.
issues.conclusion: In substance, the agreement was a lease, not a licence, and therefore did not satisfy the licence condition for retention under Section 6(1)(i).
issues.legal_principle: The substance of a transaction, rather than its label or form, determines whether it is a lease or licence. Under Sections 105 and 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a right to enjoy immovable property for a term in return for consideration may constitute a lease; Sections 3 of that Act and 3(26) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, support treating an interest in land or a benefit arising from land as immovable property. A right to work mineral land and appropriate the mineral is a right to enjoy that property. The Court approved Balakrishna Pal v. Jagannath Marwari, applied Nageshwar Bux Roy v. Bengal Coal Company, and approved Commissioner of Income Tax, Bihar and Orissa v. Kumar Kanakhaya Narain Singh; it distinguished the contrary reasoning in Gowan v. Christie and Raj Kumar Thakur Girdhari Singh v. Megh Lal Pandey and differed from H. V. Low & Co. Ltd. v. Jyoti Prasad Singh Deo.

rule.if: grant_classification_dispute and mineral_extraction_right_granted and fixed_periodic_consideration and exclusive_possession_for_defined_term

predicates.grant_classification_dispute: The proceeding requires the court to determine whether an agreement granting rights over land is a lease or a licence.
predicates.mineral_extraction_right_granted: The agreement authorizes the grantee to extract, remove and appropriate a mineral from the land.
predicates.fixed_periodic_consideration: The grantee must make a fixed payment at recurring intervals, independent of the quantity of mineral extracted.
predicates.exclusive_possession_for_defined_term: The agreement allows the grantee to occupy the land exclusively for a defined term before possession returns to the grantor.

issues.definition: When an agreement in a classification dispute grants mineral-extraction rights for fixed recurring consideration and exclusive possession for a defined term, the transaction is a lease.
